Доктор Вольф похищает возлюбленную главного героя, что побуждает его к решительным действиям по её освобождению. Сюжет начинается с пробуждения героя в изолированной пещере, где он не знает, где находится его спутница.

По мере развития сюжета герой раскрывает сложную иерархическую структуру, созданную доктором Вольфом. Эта структура напоминает квазигосударственное образование по своей организации и масштабам. Доктор Вольф демонстрирует высокий уровень стратегического мышления и значительные ресурсы, что превосходит ожидания героя.

Игроку предстоит пройти через испытания, которые включают физическое противостояние с вооружёнными силами, подчинёнными доктору Вольфу, а также решение интеллектуальных задач, требующих анализа и принятия взвешенных решений.

I played mostly for the nostalgia value from back when the original game was on flash.
Biggest thing for me is, the controls are not great. It's not very responsive, death animations are slow, landing surfaces are very small and unforgiving at times, and the leap... I wish there was an easy way to tell how much I'm going to be dashing, because it's an important mechanic. It helps you move faster horizontally, but doesn't tell you where you'll land, which is frustrating.
It teaches you to think and solve puzzles, then it makes you do precision platforming, then suddenly there's a boss fight, then there's stealth section with unclear lines of sight... it's kind of all over the place and there are certainly good stuff in there, but hard to say that the overall experience is enjoyable.
Aesthetics are pretty neat, with the blood falling off through the floors, that I must admit. It's a bit goofy when there's blood dripping from the ceilings and the enemies are completely oblivious though.

I didn't know it was going to be so difficult having played the original flash game and seeing it wasn't THAT bad. And yet, the game not only demands precision platforming, but also has the nerve to make you build and lose velocity where your character doesn't stop or start moving immediately, causing you to conveniently slide into the many obstacles it will throw your way, as if dying upon being hit wasn't punishing enough. The last straw was this room full of lasers and an acid pool with narrow platforms to jump on, which gives you the smallest margin for error. It is very frustrating. If I had known Vox Populi Vox Dei 2 was going to be some B.S. like "I Wanna Be The Guy", I would have never bought it in the first place.

Play this game if you like B.S. difficulty platform games.

A followup platfomer to the first game. 

I'll admit, i'm sad that the third game will likely never happen and I'll never get closure to the story, but that is tangentially relevant to my review of this game. 

This game expands the story of the first game while removing/changing the focus of a lot of the gameplay from making tough choices of which werewolf to gore first(and to gore them quickly/carefully) to fast and precise platforming that requires a lot of trial and error. 
Missing a jump means death 99% of the time. 
There is a flying minigame section near the end of the game which alone costs about 1 hour on your first playthrough. 10 minutes of learning how to use the bird you ride on, 50 minutes of memorizing the patterns of all the bullet hell things coming at you and killing those things as they come on screen. Thankfully the game has frequent checkpoints during this section, but still. 
 The final sequence is very well done and super interesting, but my problem with it is how it suggests the third game is going to be coming soon and very much hypes up the possibility of this world of machine-gun-chest werewolves versus a singular ninja, trying to take her kid to safety, and all of a sudden there happens to be this singular *GOOD* werewolf who saved her?!

Frankly, I would call that a spoiler but this game is from 2015 and the reveal doesn't matter unless you played through the first game(which isn't on steam). 

Heck, I don't even know if the developers are still... well... alive. 

in any case, 7/10. Worth the 3 dollars.

If you're looking for the experience the first episode had to offer, you won't find it here. While the nostalgia factor is definitely here, the game feels very different from the first episode of the series, focusing mainly around platforming segments, rather than interaction with the enemies. 

Core mechanics from the first game are still present, pounce being the only way to deal with enemies at the same time being a useful movement tool.


There are some segments of the game which require pure luck to pass through if it is your first time in a certain area, as if the game is softly encouraging player's death, boss fights could serving as an example, the first time you face the first boss you have no idea which part of the floor is going to open first, therefore you have to make a 50/50 guess to pick a side you're going to attack from.

Music is amazing, I absolutely adore it, especially during first levels of the game and the airborne segment, sadly soundtrack can't save a mediocre game.

I sincerely hope that if the third part is ever released, which is quite doubtful, it'll allow more ways of dealing with enemies, as well as changing the focus from a common platformer feel to actual Vox Populi Vox Dei that we had a chance to see in the first episode.

This game is frustratingly close to being good. It's set up in a similar vein to Super Meat Boy(in fact, it's even a sequel to a flash-based game as well) and features many of the same ideas and concepts. Namely, do platforming puzzles that kill you frequently until you have them down pat and can progress. The levels and designs are on the bland and minimal side(there's only one type of repeated enemy in the entire game) but not in a bad way. Unfortunately the controls feel loose in a way a game like this should not be.  

The game is short, being about 50-odd 'levels'(single screens with 4-6 sections of traps, jumps, and obstacles to overcome), with the final level being a blind-faith 'invisible' portion that was particularly onerous considering the loose controls.

For the sequel to a flash game from quite a long time ago, I had low expectations when I saw VPVD2 on Steam. But I really liked the flash game, and it was on sale for like 3 bucks, so I figured I had nothing to lose... but 3 bucks.

I wasn't too surprised however, when the game actually looked really pretty, keeping in mind it's pixelated style, and contrast to the first one. And on top of it, boasted tight responsive controls and interesting, though not too difficult, puzzles, many of which present themselves in the form of boss fights.

In the end, though, the game is on the cheaper side because of it's length. It's a relatively short experience, but a pretty solid one regardless.

Скажу сразу, игра не смогла "зацепить" в начале повествования своей атмосферой, а механики игры окончательно оттолкнули меня от её прохождения и дальнейшего погружения в неё.

А теперь подробнее.
Самый главный минус игры для меня - это механики игры и проблемы с плавным увеличением сложности. Вот ты просто бегаешь и "забиваешь" врагов кулаками (анимация и озвучка при этом, как по мне, слишком затянута и отталкивает, маленький минус в копилку), и вот ты уже на супер уровне, с кучей ловушек, параллельным двойником, лавой и прочей сопутствующей механикой, желающей тебя убить. Слишком резко, слишком большой минус для меня. Нет плавного увеличения сложности, соответственно нет плавного погружения в игру.

Вторая большая проблема это хитбоксы. Устал умирать от соприкосновения с моей аурой невидимых пикселей, хитбоксов враждебных механик.

Третий минус - медленная анимация движения персонажа в тех моментах, где всё вокруг тебя движется с быстрой или нормальной скоростью. Несоответствие анимаций на экране, которое ни чем не оправдано, вроде персонаж выпил немного яда, поэтому и "страдает" его управление. Это ощущение, будто ты играешь за персонажа "под веществами", да просто потому что вот так, сильно утомляет.

И четвёртый минус - это сюжет. Хотя бы самый минимальный. По ходу прохождения явно видно, что это какой-то мир, в нём есть его жители, но кто? что? зачем? Бегать по платформеру просто потому что это платформер, да ещё и с "кривыми" механиками, быстро утомляет.

Это всё в совокупности отбило моё желание проходить игру дальше, после нескольких начальных уровней.

Как любитель хардкорных платформеров, вроде Celeste, я ценю когда в игре есть так называемый "хардкор", и когда правильное использование механик помогают тебе его преодолеть. Но когда в игре "хардкор" заключается в управлении "кривыми" механиками и всеми сопутствующими проблемами игры в целом, то играть в такую игру становится скучно.

Vox Populi Vox Dei 2 is the continuation of a free online Flash game. When I discovered it, this fact both excited me and put me a little on edge as the only other thing under this developer's belt, that I know of, was said Flash game. Nevertheless, I paid the $3 in baited anticipation, as the original is a great little game experience on its own. Unfortunately, my gut was mostly right to be cautious about the sequel. Vox 2 ultimately amounts to a generic, though decently made, indie platformer. The original's claim to fame was its physics and method of dispatching your enemies, as you were to tackle them, eviscerate them mercilessly, then reposition yourself to assure you weren't exposed. The challenge was in the killing method taking several seconds and leaving you vulnerable to attack. The levels were mostly based around timing your jumps so that you could tackle an enemy either without being seen or attacking in such a way that landed you behind cover safe from enemy attack. The original also had a stealth mechanic which allowed you to sneak past enemies. It wasn't truly critical to beat the game, but it did allow for less tedious success. It's worth noting that Vox 2 arbitrarily tears this stealth mechanic away from the player early on and, as far as I can tell, never restores it. For the most part Vox 2 strays from the original's design philsophy in exchange for a less interesting and more frustrating focus on precision platforming. There's nothing inherently wrong with altering a game's direction, but Vox 2 really doesn't do anything special with its new calling. The game's bones are fundamentally janky, with respawn animations throwing off your timing as you try to set a pattern for yourself level after level. This is paired with questionable level design and controls that feel ever so slightly less responsive than a player would want for this type of game. The positives of the game's core are reduced, as well. In the first Vox, your tackle sent werewolves sliding on their back across the screen as you ripped them open, giving a real sense of heft and momentum. Here you fly back a few feet, then stop dead on the ground. On top of that, the kill method now requires you to hit the space bar repeatedly instead of simply holding it down as you could in the first game. Being that this is the only real thing carried over from the first game, it's a shame that it is made so much more tedious, less satisfying, and less prevalent. The game does attempt to vary the basic precision platforming with other mechanics, such as a horizontal flight section. Similarly to the rest of its gameplay, however, Vox 2 doesn't do anything especially interesting or satisfying with these sections. Part of the reason Vox 2 seems to have sacrificed so much of its gameplay is in the name of its aesthetics and storytelling. This isn't entirely without merit, as the game sees you travelling a vast distance through fairly varied environments, which does convey a certain sense of wonder. QUICK SPOILER: This is really to no end, though, as there is no final cutscene, text screen, or render of your character having overcome his trials. All you are rewarded with is a stylized "to be continued" screen. END SPOILER. With Vox 2 having soiled its predecessor's merits, introducing a new gameplay philosophy that isn't engaging, and totalling a less than 2 hour experience, Vox 2 doesn't outshine its predecessor. If anything, it makes you want to replay it instead.

TLDR: Rage oriented platformer with gore and some half decent animations. Decent controls. Repetitive, tedious and restrictive gameplay loop. 

The game was a centered window with 4 frames on all side. While the controls were solid, everything was obviously put at the service of the gameplay. With a tiny protagonist sprite, large open fields of view. There are specific sequences of actions that have to be performed in a strict manner, with usually few ways of doing things differently. For example, it might be necessary to jump at the near end of a platform, so you can use the dash attack on a foe, so his body prevents you from falling on the other side, so you can then climb to the higher platform, rather than plummet down. In another instance I had to dodge a bunch of insta-death rocks and avoid pre-scripted insta death events. There is little to no advance notice from some deaths, such as traps and the like, and the minimalist game engine does not help matters much either.

The main core problem is that the game is not very engaging, there is no story, the audiovisuals are flash game grade, and while the blood and animations are neat, there is not a lot of variety to it, and it is stuff we have seen in other games. In fact you would be probably better off playing or replaying those other games rather than playing this. Still, strictly mechanically speaking it works as intended, and there is honest platforming challenges in there. It is just that I get bored, disengage, and start making mistakes, which then forces me to restart, bores me further, and creates a vicious cycle. Other players with a much better grasp of motor control and muscle memory will breeze through huge portions of this probably with much less effort and much more enjoyment, and probably yield a play session out of it at most until they beat it. The duration really depends on the skill ceiling of the player. 

The sound design was also disappointingly basic, with no music and very limited FX for attack and jump.
